title: 1 Thessalonians

stories.title: 📜 1 Thessalonians 1
summaryBullets: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, To the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace and peace to you. (1:1).
We always thank God for all of you, remembering you in our prayers (1:2).
and continually recalling before our God and Father your work of faith, your labor of love, and your enduring hope in our Lord Jesus Christ. (1:3).
Brothers who are beloved by God, we know that He has chosen you, (1:4).
because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power, in the Holy Spirit, and with great conviction — just as you know we lived among you for your sake. (1:5).
And you became imitators of us and of the Lord when you welcomed the message with the joy of the Holy Spirit, in spite of your great suffering. (1:6).
As a result, you have become an example to all the believers in Macedonia and Achaia. (1:7).
For not only did the message of the Lord ring out from you to Macedonia and Achaia, but your faith in God has gone out to every place, so that we have no need to say anything more. (1:8).
For they themselves report what kind of welcome you gave us, and how you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God (1:9).
and to await His Son from heaven, whom He raised from the dead — Jesus our deliverer from the coming wrath. (1:10).
crossRefs: Romans 1:8: Faith proclaimed in all the world.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּשׂוֹרָה (bəśōrāh), Greek: εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion, NT), Aramaic: סַבּוּרְתָא (sabbūrtā)
translationNotes.note: Literally 'good news'; in the NT refers to the proclamation of salvation through Jesus Christ.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֵמָה (ḥēmāh), Greek: ὀργή (orgē, NT), Aramaic: רוגזא (rūgzā)
translationNotes.note: Term for anger or judgment; here denotes God’s coming judgment.

Thessalonica was the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia, a port on the Thermaic Gulf sitting on the Egnatian Way, the paved road that ran from the Adriatic to Byzantium, and it kept the standing of a free city with its own council and magistrates. Luke calls those magistrates politarchs (Acts 17:6-8), a title that appears nowhere in classical Greek literature. It turns up on the stones: inscriptions from Thessalonica and elsewhere in Macedonia use exactly that word for the city's board of officials, one of them from a gate of the city now in the British Museum.

Turning from idols in 1:9 was not a change of private opinion. The gods were built into a city's public life: sacrifices opened council meetings, trade guilds dined in temple rooms, family celebrations began with an offering, and the emperor was honoured with the rest. Thessalonica had the Greek gods, the Egyptian gods Serapis and Isis, whose sanctuary is attested there by inscriptions, and the local cult of Cabirus. A man who stopped attending withdrew from his guild, his neighbours' tables, and the city's calendar at once, which is why 1:6 speaks of severe suffering in the same breath.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul thanks God for the Thessalonians’ faith, love, and hope, their turning from idols, and their witness as they await Jesus’ return.

stories.title: 🌿 1 Thessalonians 2
summaryBullets: You yourselves know, brothers, that our visit to you was not in vain. (2:1).
As you are aware, we had already endured suffering and shameful treatment in Philippi. But in the face of strong opposition, we were bold in our God to speak to you the gospel of God. (2:2).
For our appeal does not arise from deceit or ulterior motives or trickery. (2:3).
Instead, we speak as those approved by God to be entrusted with the gospel, not in order to please men but God, who examines our hearts. (2:4).
As you know, we never used words of flattery or any pretext for greed. God is our witness! (2:5).
Nor did we seek praise from you or from anyone else, although as apostles of Christ we had authority to demand it. (2:6).
On the contrary, we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother caring for her children. (2:7).
We cared so deeply that we were delighted to share with you not only the gospel of God, but our own lives as well. That is how beloved you have become to us. (2:8).
Surely you recall, brothers, our labor and toil. We worked night and day so that we would not be a burden to anyone while we proclaimed to you the gospel of God. (2:9).
You are witnesses, and so is God, of how holy, righteous, and blameless our conduct was among you who believed. (2:10).
For you know that we treated each of you as a father treats his own children— (2:11).
encouraging you, comforting you, and urging you to walk in a manner worthy of God, who calls you into His own kingdom and glory. (2:12).

And we continually thank God because, when you received the word of God that you heard from us, you accepted it not as the word of men, but as it truly is, the word of God, which is also now at work in you who believe. (2:13).
For you, brothers, became imitators of the churches of God in Judea that are in Christ Jesus. You suffered from your own countrymen the very things they suffered from the Jews, (2:14).
who killed both the Lord Jesus and their own prophets and drove us out as well. They are displeasing to God and hostile to all men, (2:15).
hindering us from telling the Gentiles how they may be saved. As a result, they continue to heap up their sins to full capacity; the utmost wrath has come upon them. (2:16).
Brothers, although we were torn away from you for a short time (in person, not in heart), our desire to see you face to face was even more intense. (2:17).
For we wanted to come to you — indeed I, Paul, tried again and again — but Satan obstructed us. (2:18).
After all, who is our hope, our joy, our crown of boasting, if it is not you yourselves in the presence of our Lord Jesus at His coming? (2:19).
You are indeed our glory and our joy. (2:20).
crossRefs: Acts 16:22-24: Paul and Silas beaten in Philippi.
Galatians 1:10: Seeking to please God, not man.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֶבְרָה (ʿeḇrāh), Greek: ὀργή (orgē, NT), Aramaic: רגזא (rāgzā)
translationNotes.note: Another Hebrew term for fierce anger, often used in prophetic contexts of divine judgment.

Manual work was a social position, and it was low. Cicero sets out the ranking in his book on duties: the wages of a hired workman are the price of slavery, and there is nothing free about a workshop (De Officiis 1.150-151). Teachers of philosophy avoided it by charging fees or living off a wealthy patron. Paul's trade in Acts 18:3 was cutting and stitching leather for tents and awnings, heavy work with an awl and a knife, and a day's labour was worth a denarius (Matthew 20:2). He tells the Thessalonians in 2:9 that he did it at night as well as by day so that no one there had to keep him.

The word in 2:7 is not mother but nurse: the woman hired to feed and raise another household's infant. Contracts for the work survive on papyrus from Egypt, running two or three years at a monthly wage, with clauses about the nurse's diet and conduct. Paul sharpens it by saying she is caring for her own children, and then turns the image round in 2:11 to a father dealing with his own sons.

Two different objects come into English as crown. A diadema is a ruler's headband, the mark of a king. A stephanos, the word in 2:19, is a wreath: the circle of leaves put on the winner's head at the games, worth nothing as material and everything as public recognition, and it withered within days. Greek cities also voted a wreath to a citizen as a civic honour, announced in the theatre.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul recalls his sincere ministry, his parental care, and the Thessalonians’ imitation of suffering churches, noting opposition and God’s judgment on those hindering the gospel.

stories.title: 📜 1 Thessalonians 3
summaryBullets: So when we could bear it no longer, we were willing to be left on our own in Athens. (3:1).
We sent Timothy, our brother and fellow worker for God in the gospel of Christ, to strengthen and encourage you in your faith, (3:2).
so that none of you would be shaken by these trials. For you know that we are destined for this. (3:3).
Indeed, when we were with you, we kept warning you that we would suffer persecution; and as you know, it has come to pass. (3:4).
For this reason, when I could bear it no longer, I sent to find out about your faith, for fear that the tempter had somehow tempted you and that our labor might have been in vain. (3:5).
But just now, Timothy has returned from his visit with the good news about your faith, your love, and the fond memories you have preserved, longing to see us just as we long to see you. (3:6).
For this reason, brothers, in all our distress and persecution, we have been reassured about you, because of your faith. (3:7).
For now we can go on living, as long as you are standing firm in the Lord. (3:8).
How can we adequately thank God for you in return for our great joy over you in His presence? (3:9).
Night and day we pray most earnestly that we may see you face to face and supply what is lacking in your faith. (3:10).
Now may our God and Father Himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you. (3:11).
And may the Lord cause you to increase and overflow with love for one another and for everyone else, just as our love for you overflows, (3:12).
so that He may establish your hearts in blamelessness and holiness before our God and Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all His saints. Amen. (3:13).
crossRefs: Romans 1:11: Paul longs to see them to impart strength.
1 Corinthians 16:9: A wide door with many adversaries.
2 Corinthians 11:14: Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָּׂטָן (śāṭān), Greek: Σατανᾶς (Satanâs, NT), Aramaic: סָטָנָא (sāṭānā)
translationNotes.note: Name meaning 'adversary'; here describing obstruction of Paul’s desire to visit.

Athens in 3:1 was long past its power and living on its reputation, a university town of philosophers, lecture halls, and monuments, with the Areopagus council still meeting and statues everywhere (Acts 17:16-22). Paul reached it alone after being run out of Thessalonica and then Berea, and he waited there for Silas and Timothy. Sending Timothy back cost him his only companion in a city where he knew nobody.

Thessalonica to Athens is roughly three hundred miles by road. A man on foot covered about twenty miles a day, so Timothy's journey there and back, plus the time he stayed, accounts for the long silence Paul describes in 2:17-3:6. There was no postal service for private letters; the imperial courier system carried government traffic only. Ordinary people sent letters by a friend, a household slave, or a merchant heading the right way, which is why Paul names his carriers: Timothy here, Tychicus in Colossians 4:7-8, Phoebe in Romans 16:1-2.

The word repeated through 3:3-7 is a pressing word. Its root sense is weight bearing down, the pressure of a crowd or a press squeezing grapes, and Greek used it of being hemmed in with no room to move. English affliction and tribulation both come from Latin words that meant the same physical thing, threshing and rubbing. The picture is not sadness; it is being crushed.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul longs to see the Thessalonians again, hindered by Satan, but is comforted by Timothy’s good report and prays for their steadfast holiness until Christ’s coming.

stories.title: 🌿 1 Thessalonians 4
summaryBullets: Finally, brothers, we ask and encourage you in the Lord Jesus to live in a way that is pleasing to God, just as you have received from us. This is how you already live, so you should do so all the more. (4:1).
For you know the instructions we gave you by the authority of the Lord Jesus. (4:2).
For it is God’s will that you should be holy: You must abstain from sexual immorality; (4:3).
each of you must know how to control his own body in holiness and honor, (4:4).
not in lustful passion like the Gentiles who do not know God; (4:5).
and no one should ever violate or exploit his brother in this regard, because the Lord will avenge all such acts, as we have already told you and solemnly warned you. (4:6).
For God has not called us to impurity, but to holiness. (4:7).
Anyone, then, who rejects this command does not reject man but God, the very One who gives you His Holy Spirit. (4:8).
Now about brotherly love, you do not need anyone to write to you, because you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another. (4:9).
And you are indeed showing this love to all the brothers throughout Macedonia. But we urge you, brothers, to excel more and more (4:10).
and to aspire to live quietly, to attend to your own matters, and to work with your own hands, as we instructed you. (4:11).
Then you will behave properly toward outsiders, without being dependent on anyone. (4:12).
Brothers, we do not want you to be uninformed about those who sleep in death, so that you will not grieve like the rest, who are without hope. (4:13).
For since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, we also believe that God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep in Him. (4:14).
By the word of the Lord, we declare to you that we who are alive and remain until the coming of the Lord will by no means precede those who have fallen asleep. (4:15).
For the Lord Himself will descend from heaven with a loud command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God, and the dead in Christ will be the first to rise. (4:16).
After that, we who are alive and remain will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. And so we will always be with the Lord. (4:17).
Therefore encourage one another with these words. (4:18).
crossRefs: Hebrews 12:14: Strive for holiness without which none will see the Lord.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קִדּוּשׁ (qidduš, sense), Greek: ἁγιασμός (hagiasmós, NT), Aramaic: קדושתא (qdūšṯā)
translationNotes.note: Process of being set apart to God; here applied to holy living, especially in sexual purity.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שׁוֹפָר (shofar) - Hebrew: חֲצֹצְרָה (chatsotserah) - Greek: σάλπιγξ (salpinx)
translationNotes.note: Israel had two instruments behind the one English word. The shofar is a ram's horn, and it is what sounded at Sinai, growing louder and louder until the people begged it to stop (Exodus 19:16, 19). The chatsotserah is a straight trumpet of hammered silver; Numbers 10:1-10 orders two of them and assigns each signal a meaning: one trumpet summons the leaders, two summon the whole assembly, a short blast breaks camp, and an alarm calls out the army. They were also blown over the sacrifices at the appointed feasts and new moons, and the first day of the seventh month was marked by blowing them (Leviticus 23:24).

The phrase in 4:17 uses a term with a fixed public sense: when a ruler or dignitary approached a city, a delegation of citizens went out along the road to meet him and then escorted him back in. Luke describes it happening to Paul in Acts 28:15, where the believers came out from Rome as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet him and walked back with him. The same word is used of the virgins going out to meet the bridegroom in Matthew 25:6.

The verb for dying in 4:13-15 is the ordinary word for going to sleep, and the noun built from it, koimeterion, a sleeping place, is where English gets cemetery. Jewish practice was burial in the ground or in a rock-cut tomb, with the bones gathered into a stone box a year later where family tombs were used. The Roman world mostly burned its dead, and poorer people joined burial societies that took monthly dues so that a member would not go into a common pit. Paul is writing to people who had recently buried someone.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul exhorts the Thessalonians to holiness, sexual purity, and brotherly love, instructing them to live quietly and work responsibly before outsiders.

stories.title: 🕊️ 1 Thessalonians 5
summaryBullets: Now about the times and seasons, brothers, we do not need to write to you. (5:1).
For you are fully aware that the Day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. (5:2).
While people are saying, “Peace and security,” destruction will come upon them suddenly, like labor pains on a pregnant woman, and they will not escape. (5:3).
But you, brothers, are not in the darkness so that this day should overtake you like a thief. (5:4).
For you are all sons of the light and sons of the day; we do not belong to the night or to the darkness. (5:5).
So then, let us not sleep as the others do, but let us remain awake and sober. (5:6).
For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk, get drunk at night. (5:7).
But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love, and the helmet of our hope of salvation. (5:8).
For God has not appointed us to suffer wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ. (5:9).
He died for us so that, whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with Him. (5:10).
Therefore encourage and build one another up, just as you are already doing. (5:11).
But we ask you, brothers, to acknowledge those who work diligently among you, who care for you in the Lord and who admonish you. (5:12).
In love, hold them in highest regard because of their work. Live in peace with one another. (5:13).
And we urge you, brothers, to admonish the unruly, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with everyone. (5:14).
Make sure that no one repays evil for evil. Always pursue what is good for one another and for all people. (5:15).
Rejoice at all times. (5:16).
Pray without ceasing. (5:17).
Give thanks in every circumstance, for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus. (5:18).
Do not extinguish the Spirit. (5:19).
Do not treat prophecies with contempt, (5:20).
but test all things. Hold fast to what is good. (5:21).
Abstain from every form of evil. (5:22).
Now may the God of peace Himself sanctify you completely, and may your entire spirit, soul, and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. (5:23).
The One who calls you is faithful, and He will do it. (5:24).
Brothers, pray for us as well. (5:25).
Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss. (5:26).
I charge you before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers. (5:27).
The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. (5:28).
crossRefs: 1 Corinthians 15:51-52: Resurrection and change at the last trumpet.
Matthew 24:42-44: The coming of the Son of Man like a thief.
John 14:3: Jesus promises to take his own to be with him.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יָשֵׁן (yāšēn), Greek: κοιμάομαι (koimáomai, NT), Aramaic: דמיך (damīḵ)
translationNotes.note: Used as a euphemism for death in biblical texts.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תָּפַשׂ (tāfaś, sense), Greek: ἁρπάζω (harpázō, NT), Aramaic: חטף (ḥaṭap)
translationNotes.note: Means to seize or snatch suddenly; used of believers being taken up to meet the Lord.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יוֹם־יְהוָה (yōm YHWH), Greek: ἡμέρα κυρίου (hēméra kyríou, NT), Aramaic: יומא דמריא (yōmā d-māryā)
translationNotes.note: Phrase in prophets for God’s decisive time of judgment and salvation; used here for Christ’s return.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul comforts believers that the dead in Christ will rise and the living will be caught up with them at the Lord’s return, warning them to stay watchful and sober until that day.

intro:
1 Thessalonians was written by Paul the apostle (1 Thessalonians 1:1), with Silvanus (the Latinized form of Silas) and Timothy named as co-greeters. The letter was composed in Corinth around AD 50-51, during Paul's eighteen-month stay there at the end of his second missionary journey (Acts 18:1-18); it is one of Paul's earliest surviving letters, second only to Galatians under the early-date view of that letter. Paul had founded the Thessalonian church only months earlier on the same missionary journey (Acts 17:1-9). After Paul, Silas, and Timothy had been beaten with rods and imprisoned in Philippi (Acts 16:22-24), they were released and traveled west along the Via Egnatia roughly a hundred miles to Thessalonica, the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia. Paul preached in the Thessalonian synagogue for three consecutive Sabbaths (Acts 17:2), with significant fruit among Jews, "devout Greeks" (God-fearers attached to the synagogue), and prominent women of the city. Jewish opposition organized a mob attack against the house of Jason where Paul was staying (Acts 17:5-9); when the mob could not find Paul and Silas, they dragged Jason before the city authorities (called "politarchs" in Acts 17:6 and 17:8, a Greek title for Thessalonian magistrates that was once thought to be a Lukan error until archaeological inscriptions from Thessalonica confirmed it as the precise civic title used in the city). The Christians sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, where Jewish opposition from Thessalonica caught up with them; Paul was then escorted to Athens while Silas and Timothy stayed behind in Berea (Acts 17:10-15). From Athens Paul sent Timothy back to Thessalonica to check on the persecuted young church (1 Thessalonians 3:1-5); Timothy returned to Paul in Corinth with encouraging news that the Thessalonians were standing firm (1 Thessalonians 3:6-8), prompting Paul to write 1 Thessalonians as his reply. Paul (originally Saul) was born in Tarsus of Cilicia around AD 5-10 to a Hebrew family of the tribe of Benjamin, educated in Jerusalem under Gamaliel the Pharisee before his conversion on the Damascus road and his apostolic ministry to the Gentiles; he was martyred by beheading in Rome under Nero around AD 66-67 (see the introduction to Romans for the full biographical sketch).

The historical setting is the city of Thessalonica in the Roman province of Macedonia. Thessalonica had been founded in 315 BC by the Macedonian general Cassander, who named the city after his wife Thessalonike, the half-sister of Alexander the Great (her own name combined Thessaly with nike, "victory in Thessaly," commemorating a Macedonian battle). The city sat at a strategic location at the head of the Thermaic Gulf on the Aegean Sea and on the great east-west Roman road called the Via Egnatia, which ran from Dyrrachium on the Adriatic coast across the Balkans to Byzantium on the Bosporus. This combination of maritime and overland trade made Thessalonica the largest and wealthiest city of Macedonia, with a population estimated at 200,000 in Paul's day. The city had been granted the status of a libera civitas (free city) under Augustus in 42 BC for siding with Antony and Octavian at the Battle of Philippi; this self-governing status meant Thessalonica was administered by its own elected politarchs rather than directly by Roman appointees, though the province itself was governed by a Roman proconsul. The city had a significant Jewish community with a synagogue (Acts 17:1) and a substantial population of "God-fearing" Gentiles who attended synagogue without converting fully to Judaism. The Roman emperor at the time of writing was Claudius (AD 41-54), who in AD 49 had issued the edict expelling the Jews from Rome (the same edict that drove Aquila and Priscilla to Corinth, where Paul met them, Acts 18:2). Modern Thessaloniki (Greek Θεσσαλονίκη) is the second-largest city of Greece and has been continuously inhabited since Cassander's founding.

1 Thessalonians is the fifty-second book of the Christian Bible, the thirteenth book of the New Testament, and the eighth of Paul's thirteen letters in canonical order. The letter has five chapters. The earliest surviving manuscript is Papyrus 46 (P46, c. AD 175-225), which contains 1 Thessalonians on the same Pauline codex as the rest of the corpus; other early witnesses include Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (both 4th century AD). Notable passages include 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18, the most explicit New Testament passage on the return of Christ for His church and the resurrection of believers ("For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God. And the dead in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord"); 1 Thessalonians 5:1-11 on the unexpected timing of the day of the Lord ("like a thief in the night"); and the rapid-fire concluding commands of 1 Thessalonians 5:16-22 ("Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you. Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good. Abstain from every form of evil").
